scope: Genesis 46–50, all 146 public verses. Prior revisions remain unchanged.

source.verse_hash_method: SHA-256 of the exact UTF-8 <verse ...>...</verse> substring, including markup, whitespace, written forms, and any reading notes. No XML reserialization or Hebrew normalization.
source.public_versification_note: Public and Hebrew verse numbering align throughout Genesis 46–50.

delta_method: F0 retained wording; F1 lexical; F2 syntax/idiom; F3 consequential interpretive, textual, social, or versification choice. Editorial assessments are separate from similarity scores. Independent review has not occurred.

verses.rationale: Separates departure from worship while retaining Israel, the full possessions, Beersheba, and the relationship to Isaac’s God.
verses.before: So Israel set out with all that he had and came to Beersheba, and he offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac.
verses.after: Israel set out with everything he had. When he reached Beersheba, he offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac.
verses.tsw_comparator: So Israel set out with all that he had and came to Beersheba, and he offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac.

verses.rationale: Keeps the Israel/Jacob name shift and doubled call; names the respondent for listening clarity.
verses.before: God spoke to Israel in visions of the night and said, “Jacob, Jacob.” And he said, “Here I am.”
verses.after: God spoke to Israel in visions during the night. “Jacob! Jacob!” he called. “Here I am,” Jacob answered.
verses.tsw_comparator: And God spoke to Israel in visions of the night and said, “Jacob, Jacob.” And he said, “Here I am.”

verses.rationale: Retains the divine self-identification and the geographically specific promise as the reason not to fear.
verses.before: Then he said, “I am God, the God of your father. Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for there I will make you into a great nation.
verses.after: “I am God, the God of your father,” he said. “Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt. I will make you a great nation there.
verses.tsw_comparator: Then he said, “I am God, the God of your father. Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for there I will make you into a great nation.

verses.rationale: Repeats the emphatic divine subject and ascent/descent; renders the hand-on-eyes death idiom without restricting the return promise to one fulfillment.
verses.before: I myself will go down with you to Egypt, and I myself will also bring you up again, and Joseph's hand will close your eyes.”
verses.after: I myself will go down with you to Egypt, and I myself will surely bring you back up. Joseph’s hand will close your eyes.”
verses.tsw_comparator: I myself will go down with you to Egypt, and I myself will also bring you up again, and Joseph's hand shall close your eyes.”

verses.rationale: Preserves both names, the carried family groups, and Pharaoh’s stated purpose for the wagons.
verses.before: Then Jacob arose from Beersheba. And the sons of Israel carried Jacob their father, their little ones, and their wives in the wagons that Pharaoh had sent to carry him.
verses.after: Then Jacob left Beersheba. Israel’s sons carried their father Jacob, their little ones, and their wives in the wagons Pharaoh had sent to carry him.
verses.tsw_comparator: Then Jacob arose from Beersheba. And the sons of Israel carried Jacob their father, their little ones, and their wives in the wagons that Pharaoh had sent to carry him.

verses.rationale: Keeps acquired property and livestock distinct and lets the final family phrase retain its summarizing force.
verses.before: They also took their livestock and their possessions, which they had acquired in the land of Canaan, and came into Egypt, Jacob and all his offspring with him,
verses.after: They took their livestock and the possessions they had acquired in Canaan and went to Egypt—Jacob and all his descendants with him.
verses.tsw_comparator: They also took their livestock and their possessions, which they had acquired in the land of Canaan, and came into Egypt, Jacob and all his offspring with him,

verses.rationale: Retains the plural daughters rather than correcting the narrator from the following list; makes the generations immediately intelligible.
verses.before: his sons and his sons’ sons with him, his daughters and his sons’ daughters. All his offspring he brought with him into Egypt.
verses.after: He brought his sons and grandsons, his daughters and granddaughters—all his descendants—with him to Egypt.
verses.tsw_comparator: his sons and his sons’ sons with him, his daughters and his sons’ daughters. All his offspring he brought with him into Egypt.

verses.rationale: Keeps the list introduction’s Jacob-and-sons wording and Reuben’s firstborn rank despite the later fuller household list.
verses.before: These are the names of the sons of Israel who came into Egypt, Jacob and his sons: Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn.
verses.after: These are the names of the Israelites who went to Egypt, Jacob and his sons. Reuben was Jacob’s firstborn.
verses.tsw_comparator: These are the names of the sons of Israel who came into Egypt, Jacob and his sons: Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn.

verses.rationale: Uses a compact genealogical sentence while preserving all four names in source order.
verses.before: The sons of Reuben: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.
verses.after: Reuben’s sons were Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.
verses.tsw_comparator: The sons of Reuben: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.

verses.rationale: Preserves six names and the specific maternal ethnicity attached only to Shaul.
verses.before: The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman.
verses.after: Simeon’s sons were Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, whose mother was a Canaanite.
verses.tsw_comparator: The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman.

verses.rationale: Keeps all three names and the recurring sons formula rather than varying it for novelty.
verses.before: The sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.
verses.after: Levi’s sons were Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.
verses.tsw_comparator: The sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.

verses.rationale: Separates the death notice and nested generation without dropping either dead son from the record.
verses.before: The sons of Judah: Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez, and Zerah. But Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan. And the sons of Perez were Hezron and Hamul.
verses.after: Judah’s sons were Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez, and Zerah. Er and Onan died in Canaan. Perez’s sons were Hezron and Hamul.
verses.tsw_comparator: The sons of Judah: Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez, and Zerah. But Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan. And the sons of Perez were Hezron and Hamul.

verses.rationale: Follows this source’s Job rather than harmonizing to Jashub in other family records; preserves source order.
verses.before: The sons of Issachar: Tola, Puvah, Jashub, and Shimron.
verses.after: Issachar’s sons were Tola, Puvah, Job, and Shimron.
verses.tsw_comparator: The sons of Issachar: Tola, Puvah, Jashub, and Shimron.

verses.rationale: Retains the three-name list in the same concise genealogical pattern.
verses.before: The sons of Zebulun: Sered, Elon, and Jahleel.
verses.after: Zebulun’s sons were Sered, Elon, and Jahleel.
verses.tsw_comparator: The sons of Zebulun: Sered, Elon, and Jahleel.

verses.rationale: Makes the group heading inclusive of grandchildren while retaining Dinah, the place, and the source total without silently repairing its counting difficulty.
verses.before: These are the sons of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob in Paddan-aram, together with his daughter Dinah. All his sons and daughters numbered thirty-three.
verses.after: These were Leah’s descendants. She bore her children to Jacob in Paddan-aram, including his daughter Dinah. His sons and daughters numbered thirty-three in all.
verses.tsw_comparator: These are the sons of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob in Paddan-aram, together with his daughter Dinah. All his sons and daughters numbered thirty-three.

verses.rationale: Preserves seven distinct names in their Hebrew order within the repeated list form.
verses.before: The sons of Gad: Ziphion, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi, and Areli.
verses.after: Gad’s sons were Ziphion, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi, and Areli.
verses.tsw_comparator: The sons of Gad: Ziphion, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi, and Areli.

verses.rationale: Separates Serah’s explicit sister relationship from the sons and preserves Beriah’s further generation.
verses.before: The sons of Asher: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, Beriah, and Serah their sister. And the sons of Beriah: Heber and Malchiel.
verses.after: Asher’s sons were Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, and Beriah; their sister was Serah. Beriah’s sons were Heber and Malchiel.
verses.tsw_comparator: The sons of Asher: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, Beriah, and Serah their sister. And the sons of Beriah: Heber and Malchiel.

verses.rationale: Retains Zilpah’s being given to Leah and counts descendants rather than implying she personally bore sixteen immediate children.
verses.before: These are the sons of Zilpah, whom Laban gave to Leah his daughter. These she bore to Jacob, sixteen persons.
verses.after: These were the descendants of Zilpah, whom Laban had given to his daughter Leah. Through her, sixteen people were born to Jacob.
verses.tsw_comparator: These are the sons of Zilpah, whom Laban gave to Leah his daughter. These she bore to Jacob, sixteen persons.

verses.rationale: Retains the source’s explicit wife designation and the two sons’ order.
verses.before: The sons of Rachel, Jacob’s wife: Joseph and Benjamin.
verses.after: The sons of Jacob’s wife Rachel were Joseph and Benjamin.
verses.tsw_comparator: The sons of Rachel, Jacob’s wife: Joseph and Benjamin.

verses.rationale: Makes both parents and the priest’s relationship clear without losing Egypt or the order of the sons.
verses.before: To Joseph in the land of Egypt were born Manasseh and Ephraim, whom Asenath the daughter of Potiphera priest of On bore to him.
verses.after: In Egypt, Joseph became the father of Manasseh and Ephraim. Their mother was Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, priest of On.
verses.tsw_comparator: To Joseph in the land of Egypt were born Manasseh and Ephraim, whom Asenath the daughter of Potiphera priest of On bore to him.

verses.rationale: Preserves all ten names as sons here without harmonizing their relationships or forms to later biblical genealogies.
verses.before: The sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, and Ard.
verses.after: Benjamin’s sons were Bela, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, and Ard.
verses.tsw_comparator: The sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, and Ard.

verses.rationale: Keeps the maternal grouping and exact fourteen-person total, with descendants encompassing grandchildren.
verses.before: These are the sons of Rachel, who were born to Jacob, fourteen persons in all.
verses.after: These were Rachel’s descendants born to Jacob—fourteen people in all.
verses.tsw_comparator: These are the sons of Rachel, who were born to Jacob, fourteen persons in all.

verses.rationale: Renders the plural genealogical heading naturally for its one named member without inventing further sons.
verses.before: The son of Dan: Hushim.
verses.after: Dan’s son was Hushim.
verses.tsw_comparator: The son of Dan: Hushim.

verses.rationale: Keeps all four names and the established list rhythm.
verses.before: The sons of Naphtali: Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer, and Shillem.
verses.after: Naphtali’s sons were Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer, and Shillem.
verses.tsw_comparator: The sons of Naphtali: Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer, and Shillem.

verses.rationale: Retains Bilhah’s being given and her maternal line’s seven-person total without confusing grandchildren with direct births.
verses.before: These are the sons of Bilhah, whom Laban gave to Rachel his daughter. These she bore to Jacob, seven persons in all.
verses.after: These were the descendants of Bilhah, whom Laban had given to his daughter Rachel. Through her, seven people were born to Jacob.
verses.tsw_comparator: These are the sons of Bilhah, whom Laban gave to Rachel his daughter. These she bore to Jacob, seven persons in all.

verses.rationale: Preserves bodily descent and the explicit exclusion of wives; does not recalculate the Hebrew total.
verses.before: All the persons belonging to Jacob who came into Egypt, who were his own descendants, not counting the wives of Jacob’s sons, were sixty-six persons in all.
verses.after: All those who went with Jacob to Egypt and came from his own body numbered sixty-six, not counting his sons’ wives.
verses.tsw_comparator: All the persons belonging to Jacob who came into Egypt, who were his own descendants, not counting the wives of Jacob’s sons, were sixty-six persons in all.

verses.rationale: Retains both the two already born in Egypt and the seventy-person household total, leaving the collective migration wording intact.
verses.before: And the sons of Joseph who were born to him in Egypt were two. All the persons of the house of Jacob who came into Egypt were seventy.
verses.after: Joseph had two sons born to him in Egypt. Altogether, Jacob’s household that went to Egypt numbered seventy.
verses.tsw_comparator: And the sons of Joseph who were born to him in Egypt were two. All the persons of the house of Jacob who came into Egypt were seventy.

verses.rationale: Retains the ahead/before movement and destination while allowing the arrival clause to lead into the reunion; the arranging sense of instruct/direct is noted.
verses.before: He had sent Judah ahead of him to Joseph to show the way before him into Goshen. And they came into the land of Goshen.
verses.after: Jacob sent Judah ahead to Joseph to arrange the way to Goshen. When they reached Goshen,
verses.tsw_comparator: He had sent Judah ahead of him to Joseph to show the way before him into Goshen. And they came into the land of Goshen.

verses.rationale: Clarifies Joseph as the actor throughout and preserves neck-embrace and prolonged weeping rather than a generic happy reunion.
verses.before: Then Joseph prepared his chariot and went up to meet Israel his father in Goshen. He presented himself to him and fell upon his neck and wept upon his neck a long time.
verses.after: Joseph had his chariot made ready and went up to meet his father Israel there. As soon as he appeared before him, he threw his arms around his father’s neck and wept against him for a long time.
verses.tsw_comparator: Then Joseph prepared his chariot and went up to meet Israel his father in Goshen. He presented himself to him and fell upon his neck and wept upon his neck a long time.

verses.rationale: Preserves seeing the face and Joseph’s continuing life as the reason for Israel’s death-ready statement.
verses.before: Israel said to Joseph, “Now let me die, since I have seen your face and know that you are still alive.”
verses.after: Israel said to Joseph, “Now I can die, since I have seen your face and know you are still alive.”
verses.tsw_comparator: Israel said to Joseph, “Now let me die, since I have seen your face and know that you are still alive.”

verses.rationale: Keeps the full audience and establishes a clearly nested report to Pharaoh.
verses.before: Joseph said to his brothers and to his father’s household, “I will go up and tell Pharaoh and will say to him, ‘My brothers and my father’s household, who were in the land of Canaan, have come to me.
verses.after: Then Joseph told his brothers and his father’s household, “I will go up and tell Pharaoh, ‘My brothers and my father’s household have come to me from Canaan.
verses.tsw_comparator: Joseph said to his brothers and to his father’s household, “I will go up and tell Pharaoh and will say to him, ‘My brothers and my father’s household, who were in the land of Canaan, have come to me.

verses.rationale: Preserves occupation, its background explanation, both animal groups, and all possessions in Joseph’s planned report.
verses.before: The men are shepherds, for they have been keepers of livestock, and they have brought their flocks and their herds and all that they have.’
verses.after: The men are shepherds; they have always raised livestock. They have brought their flocks and herds and everything they own.’
verses.tsw_comparator: The men are shepherds, for they have been keepers of livestock, and they have brought their flocks and their herds and all that they have.’

verses.rationale: Uses an ordinary occupational question while leaving the sentence open for Joseph’s instructed answer.
verses.before: And when Pharaoh calls you and says, ‘What is your occupation?’
verses.after: When Pharaoh calls you in and asks, ‘What work do you do?’
verses.tsw_comparator: And when Pharaoh calls you and says, ‘What is your occupation?’

verses.rationale: Keeps deferential servants distinct from later purchased slaves, ancestral continuity, and the source’s strong abomination language attributed to Egyptians.
verses.before: you will say, ‘Your servants have been keepers of livestock from our youth even until now, both we and our fathers,’ so that you may dwell in the land of Goshen, for every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians.”
verses.after: say, ‘Your servants have raised livestock from our youth until now, just as our ancestors did.’ Then you will be able to settle in Goshen, because Egyptians regard every shepherd as an abomination.”
verses.tsw_comparator: you shall say, ‘Your servants have been keepers of livestock from our youth even until now, both we and our fathers,’ so that you may dwell in the land of Goshen, for every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians.”

verses.rationale: Splits arrival and current location for oral clarity while preserving the complete possessions report.
verses.before: Then Joseph went in and told Pharaoh, “My father and my brothers, with their flocks and their herds and all that they possess, have come from the land of Canaan. Look, they are in the land of Goshen.”
verses.after: Joseph went to Pharaoh and told him, “My father and brothers have come from Canaan with their flocks, herds, and everything they own. They are now in Goshen.”
verses.tsw_comparator: Then Joseph went in and told Pharaoh, “My father and my brothers, with their flocks and their herds and all that they possess, have come from the land of Canaan. Behold, they are in the land of Goshen.”

verses.rationale: Retains the exact five representatives without supplying their identities or selection criteria.
verses.before: And from among his brothers he took five men and presented them to Pharaoh.
verses.after: He chose five of his brothers and presented them to Pharaoh.
verses.tsw_comparator: And from among his brothers he took five men and presented them to Pharaoh.

verses.rationale: Keeps Pharaoh’s question aligned with Joseph’s instruction but retains the brothers’ own shepherd wording.
verses.before: Pharaoh said to his brothers, “What is your occupation?” They said to Pharaoh, “Your servants are shepherds, both we and our fathers.”
verses.after: Pharaoh asked the brothers, “What work do you do?” They answered, “Your servants are shepherds, as our ancestors were.”
verses.tsw_comparator: Pharaoh said to his brothers, “What is your occupation?” They said to Pharaoh, “Your servants are shepherds, both we and our fathers.”

verses.rationale: Preserves the request’s resident-foreigner status, the pasture crisis, and the permission sought, rather than implying citizenship or effortless relocation.
verses.before: They said to Pharaoh, “We have come to sojourn in the land, for there is no pasture for your servants’ flocks, because the famine is severe in the land of Canaan. And now, please let your servants dwell in the land of Goshen.”
verses.after: They also said to Pharaoh, “We have come to live here as foreigners. There is no pasture for your servants’ flocks because the famine in Canaan is so severe. Please let your servants settle in Goshen.”
verses.tsw_comparator: They said to Pharaoh, “We have come to sojourn in the land, for there is no pasture for your servants’ flocks, because the famine is severe in the land of Canaan. And now, please let your servants dwell in the land of Goshen.”

verses.rationale: Retains Pharaoh’s opening acknowledgment as part of his continuing speech rather than removing it as redundant.
verses.before: Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Your father and your brothers have come to you.
verses.after: Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Your father and brothers have come to you.
verses.tsw_comparator: Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Your father and your brothers have come to you.

verses.rationale: Unfolds the permission and conditional appointment into audible clauses; capability is not narrowed to military strength.
verses.before: The land of Egypt is before you. Settle your father and your brothers in the best of the land. Let them dwell in the land of Goshen. And if you know any capable men among them, put them in charge of my livestock.”
verses.after: The land of Egypt is open to you. Settle your father and brothers in the best part of the land. Let them live in Goshen. If you know any capable men among them, put them in charge of my livestock.”
verses.tsw_comparator: The land of Egypt is before you. Settle your father and your brothers in the best of the land. Let them dwell in the land of Goshen. And if you know any capable men among them, put them in charge of my livestock.”

verses.rationale: Retains the surprising direction of blessing from Jacob to Pharaoh, with a brief note on greeting/farewell usage.
verses.before: Then Joseph brought in Jacob his father and set him before Pharaoh, and Jacob blessed Pharaoh.
verses.after: Then Joseph brought his father Jacob in and presented him to Pharaoh. Jacob blessed Pharaoh.
verses.tsw_comparator: Then Joseph brought in Jacob his father and set him before Pharaoh, and Jacob blessed Pharaoh.

verses.rationale: Renders the days-of-the-years age question in ordinary English while reserving the fuller life imagery for Jacob’s answer.
verses.before: Pharaoh said to Jacob, “How many are the days of the years of your life?”
verses.after: Pharaoh asked Jacob, “How old are you?”
verses.tsw_comparator: Pharaoh said to Jacob, “How many are the days of the years of your life?”

verses.rationale: Keeps the exact age, Jacob’s negative assessment, and repeated sojourning framework without turning it into an objective claim that his life was short.
verses.before: Jacob said to Pharaoh, “The days of the years of my sojourning are one hundred thirty years. Few and difficult have been the days of the years of my life, and they have not attained to the days of the years of the lives of my fathers in the days of their sojourning.”
verses.after: Jacob answered Pharaoh, “I have lived as a wanderer for a hundred and thirty years. The years of my life have been few and hard. They have not reached the number of years my ancestors lived in their wanderings.”
verses.tsw_comparator: And Jacob said to Pharaoh, “The days of the years of my sojourning are one hundred thirty years. Few and difficult have been the days of the years of my life, and they have not attained to the days of the years of the lives of my fathers in the days of their sojourning.”

verses.rationale: Preserves the second blessing that frames the audience and makes its repetition audible.
verses.before: Then Jacob blessed Pharaoh and went out from before Pharaoh.
verses.after: Jacob blessed Pharaoh again and left his presence.
verses.tsw_comparator: Then Jacob blessed Pharaoh and went out from before Pharaoh.

verses.rationale: Retains possession terminology, the name Rameses, and Pharaoh’s authorization without modernizing the geographic designation.
verses.before: So Joseph settled his father and his brothers and gave them a possession in the land of Egypt, in the best of the land, in the land of Rameses, as Pharaoh had commanded.
verses.after: Joseph settled his father and brothers in Egypt and gave them a landholding in the best part of the country, the region of Rameses, as Pharaoh had ordered.
verses.tsw_comparator: So Joseph settled his father and his brothers and gave them a possession in the land of Egypt, in the best of the land, in the land of Rameses, as Pharaoh had commanded.

verses.rationale: Retains the unusual little-ones basis of the provision instead of silently replacing it with a total household census.
verses.before: Joseph provided his father, his brothers, and all his father’s household with food, according to the number of their dependents.
verses.after: Joseph supplied his father, his brothers, and all his father’s household with food, according to the number of their little ones.
verses.tsw_comparator: And Joseph provided his father, his brothers, and all his father’s household with food, according to the number of their dependents.

verses.rationale: Preserves the force of the two lands’ exhaustion as the narrative shifts from Joseph’s family to the wider population.
verses.before: Now there was no food in all the land, for the famine was very severe, so that the land of Egypt and the land of Canaan languished because of the famine.
verses.after: There was no food anywhere in the land, for the famine was very severe. Egypt and Canaan wasted away because of it.
verses.tsw_comparator: Now there was no food in all the land, for the famine was very severe, so that the land of Egypt and the land of Canaan languished because of the famine.

verses.rationale: Keeps silver and its transfer to Pharaoh explicit, distinguishing resource concentration from generic successful administration.
verses.before: Joseph gathered all the silver that was found in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan in exchange for the grain that they bought. And Joseph brought the silver into Pharaoh’s house.
verses.after: Joseph collected all the silver in Egypt and Canaan as people bought grain, and he brought the silver into Pharaoh’s palace.
verses.tsw_comparator: And Joseph gathered all the silver that was found in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan in exchange for the grain that they bought. And Joseph brought the silver into Pharaoh’s house.

verses.rationale: Preserves the collective petition, the death threat of famine, and the repeated depletion of silver.
verses.before: When the silver was exhausted in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan, all the Egyptians came to Joseph and said, “Give us food. Why should we die before your eyes? For our silver is gone.”
verses.after: When the silver in Egypt and Canaan was gone, all the Egyptians came to Joseph. “Give us food!” they said. “Why should we die before your eyes? Our silver is gone.”
verses.tsw_comparator: When the silver was exhausted in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan, all the Egyptians came to Joseph and said, “Give us food. Why should we die before your eyes? For our silver is gone.”

verses.rationale: Makes the exchange explicit without describing the food as a free gift.
verses.before: Joseph said, “Give your livestock, and I will give you food in exchange for your livestock if your silver is gone.”
verses.after: Joseph answered, “Bring your livestock. If your silver is gone, I will give you food in exchange for your animals.”
verses.tsw_comparator: And Joseph said, “Give your livestock, and I will give you food in exchange for your livestock if your silver is gone.”

verses.rationale: Preserves all four livestock categories, the exchange, and the year’s complete transfer rather than collapsing the repeated accounting.
verses.before: So they brought their livestock to Joseph, and Joseph gave them food in exchange for the horses, the flocks, the herds, and the donkeys. He supplied them with food in exchange for all their livestock that year.
verses.after: So they brought their livestock to Joseph, and he gave them food in exchange for horses, sheep and goats, cattle, and donkeys. That year he kept them supplied with food in exchange for all their livestock.
verses.tsw_comparator: So they brought their livestock to Joseph, and Joseph gave them food in exchange for the horses, the flocks, the herds, and the donkeys. He supplied them with food in exchange for all their livestock that year.

verses.rationale: Keeps the year relative to the prior exchange, not automatically the famine’s second year, and names bodies and land as the remaining assets.
verses.before: When that year was ended, they came to him the following year and said to him, “We will not hide from my lord that our silver is gone, and the herds of livestock belong to my lord. There is nothing left before my lord except our bodies and our land.
verses.after: When that year ended, they came to him the following year and said, “We cannot hide it from you, my lord. Our silver is gone, and our livestock belongs to you. We have nothing left to offer you except our bodies and our land.
verses.tsw_comparator: When that year was ended, they came to him the following year and said to him, “We will not hide from my lord that our silver is gone, and the herds of livestock belong to my lord. There is nothing left before my lord except our bodies and our land.

verses.rationale: Retains the desperate proposal of purchase and enslavement, the land’s personification, and both life/death and cultivation/desolation contrasts.
verses.before: Why should we die before your eyes, both we and our land? Buy us and our land for food, and we with our land will be servants to Pharaoh. Give us seed that we may live and not die, and that the land may not be desolate.”
verses.after: Why should we perish before your eyes, both we and our land? Buy us and our land in exchange for food. We and our land will belong to Pharaoh as slaves. Give us seed so that we may live and not die, and so that the land will not become desolate.”
verses.tsw_comparator: Why should we die before your eyes, both we and our land? Buy us and our land for food, and we with our land will be servants to Pharaoh. Give us seed that we may live and not die, and that the land may not be desolate.”

verses.rationale: Preserves individual sales and the famine’s coercive pressure, with the final ownership statement kept distinct.
verses.before: So Joseph bought all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh, for every Egyptian sold his field because the famine was severe upon them. Thus the land became Pharaoh’s.
verses.after: So Joseph bought all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh. Every Egyptian sold his field because the famine had such a grip on them. The land became Pharaoh’s.
verses.tsw_comparator: So Joseph bought all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh, for every Egyptian sold his field because the famine was severe upon them. Thus the land became Pharaoh’s.

verses.rationale: Follows the pinned Masoretic reading moved-to-cities; records the important enslaved-them variant in a note rather than silently importing it.
verses.before: As for the people, he moved them into the cities from one end of the border of Egypt to the other.
verses.after: As for the people, he moved them into cities, from one end of Egypt to the other.
verses.tsw_comparator: As for the people, he moved them into the cities from one end of the border of Egypt to the other.

verses.rationale: Retains the institutional exemption and its economic reason without supplying a moral evaluation.
verses.before: Only the land of the priests he did not buy, for the priests had an allotment from Pharaoh and lived on the allotment that Pharaoh gave them. Therefore they did not sell their land.
verses.after: He did not buy the priests’ land. The priests received an allowance from Pharaoh and lived on what he gave them, so they did not sell their land.
verses.tsw_comparator: Only the land of the priests he did not buy, for the priests had an allotment from Pharaoh and lived on the allotment that Pharaoh gave them. Therefore they did not sell their land.

verses.rationale: Keeps Joseph’s explicit purchase of people as well as land, followed by seed provision, without euphemizing slavery as employment.
verses.before: Then Joseph said to the people, “Look, I have this day bought you and your land for Pharaoh. Here is seed for you, and you will sow the land.
verses.after: Joseph told the people, “Today I have bought you and your land for Pharaoh. Here is seed for you; sow the land.
verses.tsw_comparator: Then Joseph said to the people, “Behold, I have this day bought you and your land for Pharaoh. Here is seed for you, and you shall sow the land.

verses.rationale: Preserves the one-fifth/four-shares ratio and every stated use, including repeated household and child provision.
verses.before: At the harvests you will give a fifth to Pharaoh, and four parts will be your own, for seed for the field and for your food and for those of your households and as food for your little ones.”
verses.after: At harvest, give a fifth to Pharaoh. The other four shares will be yours for seed for the fields and food for yourselves, your households, and your little ones.”
verses.tsw_comparator: At the harvests you shall give a fifth to Pharaoh, and four parts shall be your own, for seed for the field and for your food and for those of your households and as food for your little ones.”

verses.rationale: Retains gratitude and slavery in the same reply; does not turn the population’s speech into the narrator’s approval of the system.
verses.before: They said, “You have saved our lives. Let us find favor in the sight of my lord, and we will be Pharaoh’s servants.”
verses.after: “You have kept us alive,” they said. “May we find favor with you, my lord. We will be Pharaoh’s slaves.”
verses.tsw_comparator: They said, “You have saved our lives. Let us find favor in the sight of my lord, and we will be Pharaoh’s servants.”

verses.rationale: Keeps the narrator’s to-this-day viewpoint, permanent levy, and land exception without asserting that the law continues into modern times.
verses.before: So Joseph made it a statute concerning the land of Egypt, and it remains to this day, that Pharaoh should have the fifth. Only the land of the priests alone did not become Pharaoh’s.
verses.after: Joseph made it a law concerning Egypt’s land that a fifth belonged to Pharaoh, and it remains in force to this day. Only the priests’ land did not become Pharaoh’s.
verses.tsw_comparator: So Joseph made it a statute concerning the land of Egypt, and it remains to this day, that Pharaoh should have the fifth. Only the land of the priests alone did not become Pharaoh’s.

verses.rationale: Retains the collective Israel and the fruitful/multiply language in contrast with surrounding land dispossession.
verses.before: Thus Israel settled in the land of Egypt, in the land of Goshen. And they gained possessions in it and were fruitful and multiplied greatly.
verses.after: Israel settled in Egypt, in the region of Goshen. They acquired holdings there, were fruitful, and increased greatly in number.
verses.tsw_comparator: Thus Israel settled in the land of Egypt, in the land of Goshen. And they gained possessions in it and were fruitful and multiplied greatly.

verses.rationale: Separates residence duration from lifespan and preserves both exact numbers.
verses.before: Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years. So the days of Jacob, the years of his life, were one hundred forty-seven years.
verses.after: Jacob lived in Egypt for seventeen years. His whole life lasted a hundred and forty-seven years.
verses.tsw_comparator: And Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years. So the days of Jacob, the years of his life, were one hundred forty-seven years.

verses.rationale: Preserves the bodily oath gesture and kindness/faithfulness pair; records its connection with the earlier Abraham oath without replacing it with a modern gesture.
verses.before: When the time drew near that Israel must die, he called his son Joseph and said to him, “If now I have found favor in your sight, put your hand under my thigh and deal with me in steadfast love and faithfulness. Do not bury me in Egypt.
verses.after: As Israel’s death drew near, he called for his son Joseph. “If I have found favor with you,” he said, “put your hand under my thigh and promise to treat me with faithful kindness. Please do not bury me in Egypt.
verses.tsw_comparator: When the time drew near that Israel must die, he called his son Joseph and said to him, “If now I have found favor in your sight, put your hand under my thigh and deal with me in steadfast love and faithfulness. Do not bury me in Egypt.

verses.rationale: Retains lying-with-ancestors death imagery, removal from Egypt, and burial location while naming Joseph’s reply.
verses.before: But let me lie with my fathers. Carry me out of Egypt and bury me in their burial place.” He answered, “I will do as you have said.”
verses.after: When I lie down with my ancestors, carry me out of Egypt and bury me in their burial place.” Joseph answered, “I will do as you say.”
verses.tsw_comparator: But let me lie with my fathers. Carry me out of Egypt and bury me in their burial place.” He answered, “I will do as you have said.”

verses.rationale: Follows the pinned bed vocalization; notes staff in the Greek tradition without changing the main text or inventing the object of the bow.
verses.before: And he said, “Swear to me.” So he swore to him. Then Israel bowed himself upon the head of the bed.
verses.after: “Swear it to me,” Jacob said. Joseph swore to him, and Israel bowed down at the head of his bed.
verses.tsw_comparator: And he said, “Swear to me.” So he swore to him. Then Israel bowed himself upon the head of the bed.

verses.rationale: Keeps the unnamed messenger unnamed and preserves the sons’ older-first order before the blessing reverses it.
verses.before: After these things, Joseph was told, “Look, your father is ill.” So he took with him his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim.
verses.after: Some time later Joseph was told, “Your father is ill.” He took his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, with him.
verses.tsw_comparator: After these things, Joseph was told, “Behold, your father is ill.” So he took with him his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim.

verses.rationale: Retains the Jacob/Israel alternation and the effort of the frail father without adding recovery.
verses.before: And when Jacob was told, “Look, your son Joseph has come to you,” Israel gathered his strength and sat up in bed.
verses.after: When Jacob was told, “Your son Joseph has come to see you,” Israel gathered his strength and sat up in bed.
verses.tsw_comparator: And when Jacob was told, “Behold, your son Joseph has come to you,” Israel gathered his strength and sat up in bed.

verses.rationale: Uses the earlier established God Almighty for El Shaddai, retaining Luz rather than substituting Bethel; uncertainty of the divine title belongs in apparatus.
verses.before: Then Jacob said to Joseph, “God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan and blessed me,
verses.after: Jacob said to Joseph, “God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in Canaan and blessed me.
verses.tsw_comparator: Then Jacob said to Joseph, “God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan and blessed me,

verses.rationale: Keeps fruitful/increase, community of peoples, descendants, and enduring land possession in Jacob’s report of the promise.
verses.before: and said to me, ‘Look, I will make you fruitful and multiply you, and I will make of you a company of peoples and will give this land to your offspring after you as an everlasting possession.’
verses.after: He told me, ‘I will make you fruitful and increase your numbers. I will make you a community of peoples and give this land to your descendants after you as an everlasting possession.’
verses.tsw_comparator: and said to me, ‘Behold, I will make you fruitful and multiply you, and I will make of you a company of peoples and will give this land to your offspring after you as an everlasting possession.’

verses.rationale: Preserves the adoption claim, its temporal boundary, and the significant Ephraim-first order with explicit comparison to Jacob’s first sons.
verses.before: And now your two sons, who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came to you in Egypt, are mine. Ephraim and Manasseh will be mine, as Reuben and Simeon are.
verses.after: So your two sons, born to you in Egypt before I came here, are mine. Ephraim and Manasseh will be mine just as Reuben and Simeon are.
verses.tsw_comparator: And now your two sons, who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came to you in Egypt, are mine. Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, as Reuben and Simeon are.

verses.rationale: Keeps subsequent children distinct from the two adopted sons and explains the name reckoning specifically within inheritance.
verses.before: But the children born to you after them will be yours. They will be called by the name of their brothers in their inheritance.
verses.after: Any children born to you after them will be yours. In their inheritance, they will be counted under their brothers’ names.
verses.tsw_comparator: But the children born to you after them shall be yours. They shall be called by the name of their brothers in their inheritance.

verses.rationale: Carries the personal force of died upon me, retains the indefinite distance and Paddan form, and does not invent a causal link between Rachel’s burial and the adoption.
verses.before: As for me, when I came from Paddan, Rachel died to my sorrow in the land of Canaan on the journey, when there was still some distance to go to Ephrath. And I buried her there on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem).”
verses.after: As for me, when I was returning from Paddan, Rachel died, to my sorrow, on the road in Canaan, while we were still some distance from Ephrath. I buried her there beside the road to Ephrath—that is, Bethlehem.”
verses.tsw_comparator: As for me, when I came from Paddan, Rachel died to my sorrow in the land of Canaan on the journey, when there was still some distance to go to Ephrath. And I buried her there on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem).”

verses.rationale: Retains seeing followed by an identification question despite the prior adoption speech; does not harmonize the narrative sequence.
verses.before: When Israel saw Joseph’s sons, he said, “Who are these?”
verses.after: Israel saw Joseph’s sons and asked, “Who are these?”
verses.tsw_comparator: When Israel saw Joseph’s sons, he said, “Who are these?”

verses.rationale: Marks the change of speaker and preserves Joseph’s acknowledgment of God and the location here.
verses.before: Joseph said to his father, “They are my sons, whom God has given me here.” And he said, “Bring them to me, please, that I may bless them.”
verses.after: “They are my sons, whom God has given me here,” Joseph told his father. “Bring them to me,” his father said, “so I can bless them.”
verses.tsw_comparator: Joseph said to his father, “They are my sons, whom God has given me here.” And he said, “Bring them to me, please, that I may bless them.”

verses.rationale: Retains the strong inability-to-see statement alongside verse 8 and names the one bringing the sons to prevent pronoun confusion. Israel is named again as the one embracing them.
verses.before: Now the eyes of Israel were dim with age, so that he could not see. So Joseph brought them near to him, and he kissed them and embraced them.
verses.after: Israel’s eyes had grown dim with age, and he could not see. Joseph brought the sons close to him, and Israel kissed and embraced them.
verses.tsw_comparator: Now the eyes of Israel were dim with age, so that he could not see. So Joseph brought them near to him, and he kissed them and embraced them.

verses.rationale: Preserves the escalation from Joseph’s face to his offspring and the attribution to God.
verses.before: Israel said to Joseph, “I never expected to see your face, and look, God has let me see your offspring also.”
verses.after: Israel said to Joseph, “I never expected to see your face again, and now God has even let me see your children.”
verses.tsw_comparator: And Israel said to Joseph, “I never expected to see your face, and behold, God has let me see your offspring also.”

verses.rationale: Makes the likely owner of the knees explicit without portraying the sons as infants or claiming a particular adoption ritual as certain.
verses.before: Then Joseph removed them from his knees, and he bowed himself with his face to the earth.
verses.after: Joseph moved them away from Israel’s knees and bowed with his face to the ground.
verses.tsw_comparator: Then Joseph removed them from his knees, and he bowed himself with his face to the earth.

verses.rationale: Preserves all four directional relations needed to understand the crossing of hands.
verses.before: Joseph took them both, Ephraim in his right hand toward Israel’s left hand, and Manasseh in his left hand toward Israel’s right hand, and brought them near him.
verses.after: Then Joseph took both sons and brought them close to Israel, with Ephraim in his right hand, toward Israel’s left, and Manasseh in his left hand, toward Israel’s right.
verses.tsw_comparator: And Joseph took them both, Ephraim in his right hand toward Israel’s left hand, and Manasseh in his left hand toward Israel’s right hand, and brought them near him.

verses.rationale: Makes the crossing visible and retains the deliberate younger/firstborn contrast; the verb’s skillful/deliberate sense is noted.
verses.before: Yet Israel stretched out his right hand and laid it upon the head of Ephraim, though he was the younger, and his left hand upon the head of Manasseh, crossing his hands, though Manasseh was the firstborn.
verses.after: But Israel stretched out his right hand and placed it on the head of Ephraim, the younger son. He placed his left hand on Manasseh’s head, crossing his hands even though Manasseh was the firstborn.
verses.tsw_comparator: But Israel stretched out his right hand and laid it upon the head of Ephraim, though he was the younger, and his left hand upon the head of Manasseh, crossing his hands, though Manasseh was the firstborn.

verses.rationale: Preserves blessing Joseph through his sons, the ancestral walk, and the shepherd image; begins poetic lineation without losing the continuous syntax.
verses.before: And he blessed Joseph and said, “The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has shepherded me all my life long to this day,
verses.after: He blessed Joseph and said, “May the God before whom my ancestors Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has shepherded me all my life to this day,
verses.tsw_comparator: And he blessed Joseph and said, “The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has shepherded me all my life long to this day,

verses.rationale: Retains angel beside the parallel divine descriptions without resolving its identity doctrinally; preserves redeem, names, and multiplication rather than adding fish to the main text.
verses.before: the angel who has redeemed me from all evil, bless the boys. And in them let my name be carried on, and the name of my fathers Abraham and Isaac. And let them multiply greatly among the earth.”
verses.after: the angel who has redeemed me from every harm, bless these young men. May my name live on in them, and the names of my ancestors Abraham and Isaac. May they increase greatly in the midst of the earth.”
verses.tsw_comparator: the angel who has redeemed me from all evil, bless the boys. And in them let my name be carried on, and the name of my fathers Abraham and Isaac. And let them multiply greatly in the midst of the earth.”

verses.rationale: Keeps Joseph’s negative response and attempted correction distinct from a completed successful transfer.
verses.before: When Joseph saw that his father laid his right hand on the head of Ephraim, it displeased him. So he took hold of his father’s hand to move it from Ephraim’s head to Manasseh’s head.
verses.after: When Joseph saw that his father had placed his right hand on Ephraim’s head, he was displeased. He took hold of his father’s hand to move it from Ephraim’s head to Manasseh’s.
verses.tsw_comparator: When Joseph saw that his father laid his right hand on the head of Ephraim, it displeased him. So he took hold of his father’s hand to move it from Ephraim’s head to Manasseh’s head.

verses.rationale: Uses natural urgent dialogue while preserving birth rank and the specific hand.
verses.before: Joseph said to his father, “Not so, my father, for this one is the firstborn. Put your right hand on his head.”
verses.after: “Not that way, Father,” Joseph said. “This one is the firstborn. Put your right hand on his head.”
verses.tsw_comparator: And Joseph said to his father, “Not so, my father, for this one is the firstborn. Put your right hand on his head.”

verses.rationale: Retains doubled knowing, both positive statements about Manasseh, and the stronger younger-son promise without mapping nations to a later political scheme.
verses.before: But his father refused and said, “I know, my son, I know. He also will become a people, and he also will be great. Even so, his younger brother will be greater than he, and his offspring will become a multitude of nations.”
verses.after: But his father refused. “I know, my son, I know,” he said. “He too will become a people, and he too will be great. Yet his younger brother will be greater than he is, and his descendants will become a multitude of nations.”
verses.tsw_comparator: But his father refused and said, “I know, my son, I know. He also shall become a people, and he also shall be great. Nevertheless, his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his offspring shall become a multitude of nations.”

verses.rationale: Clarifies the blessing formula’s function, preserves the embedded wish and reversed names, and keeps the narrator’s explanation separate from quoted poetry.
verses.before: So he blessed them that day, saying, “By you Israel will pronounce blessing, saying, ‘May God make you like Ephraim and like Manasseh.’” Thus he put Ephraim before Manasseh.
verses.after: He blessed them that day, saying, “Israel will use your names in blessings: ‘May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh.’” In this way he put Ephraim ahead of Manasseh.
verses.tsw_comparator: So he blessed them that day, saying, “By you Israel will pronounce blessing, saying, ‘May God make you like Ephraim and like Manasseh.’” Thus he put Ephraim before Manasseh.

verses.rationale: Makes the Hebrew plural you audible so the return promise is not restricted to Joseph alone.
verses.before: Then Israel said to Joseph, “Look, I am about to die, but God will be with you and will bring you again to the land of your fathers.
verses.after: Then Israel said to Joseph, “I am about to die, but God will be with you all and bring you back to the land of your ancestors.
verses.tsw_comparator: Then Israel said to Joseph, “Behold, I am about to die, but God will be with you and will bring you again to the land of your fathers.

verses.rationale: Preserves the extra portion and Jacob’s first-person claim to armed acquisition; notes Shechem wordplay and does not rewrite it to harmonize with chapters 33–34.
verses.before: Moreover, I have given to you one mountain slope more than to your brothers, which I took from the hand of the Amorite with my sword and with my bow.”
verses.after: I give you one portion more than your brothers, which I took from the Amorites with my sword and bow.”
verses.tsw_comparator: Moreover, I have given to you one mountain slope more than to your brothers, which I took from the hand of the Amorite with my sword and with my bow.”

verses.rationale: Renders the future idiom without imposing an end-of-world scheme and retains Jacob’s claim to speak about what will befall them.
verses.before: Then Jacob called his sons and said, “Gather yourselves together, that I may tell you what will happen to you in days to come.
verses.after: Jacob called his sons together and said, “Gather around, and I will tell you what will happen to you in days to come.”
verses.tsw_comparator: Then Jacob called his sons and said, “Gather yourselves together, that I may tell you what shall happen to you in days to come.

verses.rationale: Keeps both gathering and hearing commands and the parallel Jacob/Israel names in audible poetry.
verses.before: Assemble and listen, sons of Jacob; listen to Israel your father.”
verses.after: “Come together and listen, sons of Jacob; listen to Israel your father.”
verses.tsw_comparator: Assemble and listen, sons of Jacob; listen to Israel your father.”

verses.rationale: Preserves firstborn rank, bodily vigor, and the repeated superiority formula that the next verse revokes.
verses.before: “Reuben, you are my firstborn, my might and the firstfruits of my strength, preeminent in dignity and preeminent in power.
verses.after: “Reuben, you are my firstborn, my strength, the first fruit of my vigor, foremost in honor and foremost in power.
verses.tsw_comparator: “Reuben, you are my firstborn, my might and the firstfruits of my strength, preeminent in dignity and preeminent in power.

verses.rationale: Retains the water image, loss of precedence, bed violation, and abrupt second-to-third-person shift rather than smoothing away the outburst.
verses.before: Unstable as water, you will not have preeminence, because you went up to your father’s bed; then you defiled it— he went up to my couch!”
verses.after: Uncontrolled as water, you will no longer be foremost, for you went up to your father’s bed and defiled it—he went up to my couch!”
verses.tsw_comparator: Unstable as water, you shall not have preeminence, because you went up to your father’s bed; then you defiled it— he went up to my couch!”

verses.rationale: Preserves their solidarity in violence; chooses the traditional swords sense of the uncertain final noun and identifies that uncertainty in a note.
verses.before: “Simeon and Levi are brothers; weapons of violence are their swords.
verses.after: “Simeon and Levi are brothers; their swords are weapons of violence.
verses.tsw_comparator: “Simeon and Levi are brothers; weapons of violence are their swords.

verses.rationale: Preserves Jacob’s refusal of association, honor parallelism, human killing, and deliberate animal harm; collective singulars are rendered naturally as plural.
verses.before: Let my soul not enter their council; let my glory not be joined to their assembly. For in their anger they killed men, and in their self-will they hamstrung oxen.
verses.after: Let me never enter their council; let my honor never join their assembly. In their anger they killed men; at their pleasure they hamstrung oxen.
verses.tsw_comparator: Let my soul not enter their council; let my glory not be joined to their assembly. For in their anger they killed men, and in their self-will they hamstrung oxen.

verses.rationale: Keeps the curse directed at anger/fury, the first-person scattering, and the parallel national names without adding later tribal outcomes.
verses.before: Cursed be their anger, for it is fierce, and their wrath, for it is cruel. I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.”
verses.after: Cursed be their anger, so fierce, and their fury, so cruel! I will divide them within Jacob and scatter them within Israel.”
verses.tsw_comparator: Cursed be their anger, for it is fierce, and their wrath, for it is cruel. I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.”

verses.rationale: Retains praise/name wordplay in apparatus, the concrete domination image, and the broader father’s-sons formulation.
verses.before: “Judah, your brothers will praise you; your hand will be on the neck of your enemies; your father’s sons will bow down before you.
verses.after: “Judah, your brothers will praise you. Your hand will be on your enemies’ necks; your father’s sons will bow down to you.
verses.tsw_comparator: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hand shall be on the neck of your enemies; your father’s sons shall bow down before you.

verses.rationale: Preserves cub-to-adult imagery, the second/third-person alternation, prey, and the rhetorical question; does not insert an acquittal over Joseph’s sale.
verses.before: Judah is a lion’s cub; from the prey, my son, you have gone up. He stooped down; he crouched as a lion, and as a lioness— who dares rouse him?
verses.after: Judah is a lion’s cub. You have come up from the prey, my son. He crouches and lies down like a lion, like a lioness—who dares rouse him?
verses.tsw_comparator: Judah is a lion’s cub; from the prey, my son, you have gone up. He stooped down; he crouched as a lion, and as a lioness— who dares rouse him?

verses.rationale: Retains the opaque pinned Shiloh reading in the text, the two rule symbols, and peoples; notes rival construals without making one disputed messianic identification the translation.
verses.before: The scepter will not depart from Judah, nor the ruler’s staff from between his feet, until tribute comes to him, and to him will be the obedience of the peoples.
verses.after: The scepter will not leave Judah, nor the ruler’s staff from between his feet, until Shiloh comes; the obedience of peoples will be his.
verses.tsw_comparator: The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler’s staff from between his feet, until tribute comes to him, and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples.

verses.rationale: Keeps the extravagant concrete vine/donkey and wine/garment images, including blood of grapes; no prose explanation replaces the poetry.
verses.before: Binding his foal to the vine and his donkey’s colt to the choice vine, he has washed his garments in wine and his robe in the blood of grapes.
verses.after: He ties his young donkey to a vine, his donkey’s colt to a choice vine. He washes his clothes in wine, his robe in the blood of grapes.
verses.tsw_comparator: Binding his foal to the vine and his donkey’s colt to the choice vine, he has washed his garments in wine and his robe in the blood of grapes.

verses.rationale: Chooses causal with for the two min phrases while noting comparative alternatives; does not treat the verse as a literal physiological prediction.
verses.before: His eyes are darker than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk.”
verses.after: His eyes are dark with wine, his teeth white with milk.”
verses.tsw_comparator: His eyes are darker than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk.”

verses.rationale: Preserves coast, ships, and Sidon without altering the poem to fit a later territorial map.
verses.before: “Zebulun will dwell by the shore of the sea; he will become a haven for ships, and his border will be toward Sidon.”
verses.after: “Zebulun will live by the seashore, a haven for ships, with his far border toward Sidon.”
verses.tsw_comparator: “Zebulun shall dwell by the shore of the sea; he shall become a haven for ships, and his border shall be toward Sidon.”

verses.rationale: Retains the animal and bone-strength image; selects saddlebags for the disputed resting-place term with sheepfolds noted.
verses.before: “Issachar is a strong donkey, lying down between the sheepfolds.
verses.after: “Issachar is a strong-boned donkey, lying down between the saddlebags.
verses.tsw_comparator: “Issachar is a strong donkey, lying down between the sheepfolds.

verses.rationale: Preserves the movement from attractive rest and land to burden and coerced labor without turning it into cheerful service.
verses.before: He saw that a resting place was good and that the land was pleasant, so he bent his shoulder to bear and became a servant at forced labor.”
verses.after: He sees that rest is good and that the land is pleasant. He bends his shoulder to the load and becomes a forced laborer.”
verses.tsw_comparator: He saw that a resting place was good and that the land was pleasant, so he bent his shoulder to bear and became a servant at forced labor.”

verses.rationale: Retains the already clear wording after reading the Hebrew; judge preserves the Dan wordplay, and the tribe’s place in Israel remains explicit. Only poetic lineation changes.
verses.before: “Dan will judge his people as one of the tribes of Israel.
verses.after: “Dan will judge his people as one of the tribes of Israel.
verses.tsw_comparator: “Dan shall judge his people as one of the tribes of Israel.

verses.rationale: Keeps the parallel path images and the causal movement from heel bite to falling rider.
verses.before: Dan will be a serpent by the road, a viper by the path, that bites the horse’s heels so that its rider falls backward.
verses.after: Dan will be a snake beside the road, a viper along the path, biting the horse’s heels so its rider falls backward.”
verses.tsw_comparator: Dan shall be a serpent by the road, a viper by the path, that bites the horse’s heels so that its rider falls backward.

verses.rationale: Retains the abrupt first-person prayer and biblical salvation term without assigning the prayer to another speaker.
verses.before: I wait for your salvation, O LORD.”
verses.after: “I wait for your salvation, LORD.”
verses.tsw_comparator: I wait for your salvation, O LORD.”

verses.rationale: Carries the repeated raid root and rear/heel image, with the Gad wordplay noted rather than replaced with unrelated military language.
verses.before: “Raiders will raid Gad, but he will raid at their heels.”
verses.after: “Gad will be raided by raiders, but he will raid them at their heels.”
verses.tsw_comparator: “Raiders shall raid Gad, but he shall raid at their heels.”

verses.rationale: Keeps the rich food and royal delicacies parallel rather than supplying crops absent from the verse.
verses.before: “Asher’s food will be rich, and he will provide royal delicacies.”
verses.after: “Asher’s food will be rich; he will provide delicacies fit for a king.”
verses.tsw_comparator: “Asher’s food shall be rich, and he shall provide royal delicacies.”

verses.rationale: Follows the pinned doe and sayings vocalization despite the mixed imagery; notes the alternative fawns reading rather than silently changing the source.
verses.before: “Naphtali is a doe set free that bears beautiful fawns.”
verses.after: “Naphtali is a doe set free; he gives beautiful words.”
verses.tsw_comparator: “Naphtali is a doe set free that bears beautiful fawns.”

verses.rationale: Preserves the repeated fruitful phrase and spring/wall image in the traditional botanical reading; notes the competing wild-donkey interpretation of the difficult Hebrew.
verses.before: “Joseph is a fruitful branch, a fruitful branch by a spring; its branches climb over the wall.
verses.after: “Joseph is a fruitful branch, a fruitful branch beside a spring, its shoots climbing over a wall.
verses.tsw_comparator: “Joseph is a fruitful branch, a fruitful branch by a spring; its branches climb over the wall.

verses.rationale: Preserves bitter hostility, shooting, and sustained attack as distinct actions by the archers.
verses.before: The archers bitterly attacked him, shot at him, and harassed him severely,
verses.after: Archers bitterly attacked him; they shot at him and harassed him.
verses.tsw_comparator: The archers bitterly attacked him, shot at him, and harassed him severely,

verses.rationale: Preserves bow/arms and the hand image, retaining Stone rather than silently substituting Rock; makes the compressed divine-title syntax readable and notes its difficulty.
verses.before: yet his bow remained firm, and his arms were made agile by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob (from there is the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel),
verses.after: But his bow stayed firm, and his arms remained agile, by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob, by the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel,
verses.tsw_comparator: yet his bow remained firm, and his arms were made agile by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob (from there is the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel),

verses.rationale: Retains the second-person shift and all three blessing realms, including female bodily imagery; treats divine clauses as continuing the prior source of strength without adding a new speaker.
verses.before: by the God of your father, who will help you, and by the Almighty, who will bless you with blessings of heaven above, blessings of the deep that lies beneath, blessings of the breasts and of the womb.
verses.after: by the God of your father, who helps you, by the Almighty, who blesses you with blessings of heaven above, blessings of the deep lying below, blessings of breasts and womb.
verses.tsw_comparator: by the God of your father, who will help you, and by the Almighty, who will bless you with blessings of heaven above, blessings of the deep that lies beneath, blessings of the breasts and of the womb.

verses.rationale: Follows the pinned forebears construal rather than silently adopting ancient mountains; preserves hills, head/brow parallelism, and the ambiguous set-apart status in a note.
verses.before: The blessings of your father are mighty beyond the blessings of the ancient mountains, beyond the bounty of the everlasting hills. May they be upon the head of Joseph, upon the brow of him who was set apart from his brothers.”
verses.after: Your father’s blessings surpass the blessings of my forebears, reaching to the bounty of the everlasting hills. May they rest on Joseph’s head, on the brow of the one set apart from his brothers.”
verses.tsw_comparator: The blessings of your father are mighty beyond the blessings of the ancient mountains, beyond the bounty of the everlasting hills. May they be upon the head of Joseph, upon the brow of him who was set apart from his brothers.”

verses.rationale: Retains the violent wolf image and morning/evening pattern without supplying a historical identification.
verses.before: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he devours the prey, and in the evening he divides the spoil.”
verses.after: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf. In the morning he devours prey; in the evening he divides the plunder.”
verses.tsw_comparator: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he devours the prey, and in the evening he divides the spoil.”

verses.rationale: Retains the narrator’s blessing designation even for the harsh sayings and the exact twelve-tribe total.
verses.before: All these are the twelve tribes of Israel, and this is what their father spoke to them as he blessed them, blessing each with the blessing appropriate to him.
verses.after: All these are the twelve tribes of Israel. This is what their father said when he blessed them, giving each one his own blessing.
verses.tsw_comparator: All these are the twelve tribes of Israel, and this is what their father spoke to them as he blessed them, blessing each with the blessing appropriate to him.

verses.rationale: Keeps gathered-to-people distinct from burial and lets the location continue into the following verse without inventing an afterlife explanation.
verses.before: Then he commanded them and said to them, “I am about to be gathered to my people. Bury me with my fathers in the cave that is in the field of Ephron the Hittite,
verses.after: Then he gave them these instructions: “I am about to be gathered to my people. Bury me with my ancestors in the cave in the field of Ephron the Hittite,
verses.tsw_comparator: Then he commanded them and said to them, “I am about to be gathered to my people. Bury me with my fathers in the cave that is in the field of Ephron the Hittite,

verses.rationale: Preserves the full legal/geographic identification and buyer/seller relationship in two readable clauses. Uses facing Mamre consistently with the purchase account in 23:17–19.
verses.before: in the cave that is in the field of Machpelah, east of Mamre, in the land of Canaan, which Abraham bought with the field from Ephron the Hittite as property for a burial place.
verses.after: the cave in the field of Machpelah, facing Mamre in Canaan. Abraham bought the field from Ephron the Hittite as a burial property.
verses.tsw_comparator: in the cave that is in the field of Machpelah, east of Mamre, in the land of Canaan, which Abraham bought with the field from Ephron the Hittite as property for a burial place.

verses.rationale: Retains the threefold there, wives’ names, and Jacob’s first-person burial of Leah.
verses.before: There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife. There they buried Isaac and Rebekah his wife, and there I buried Leah.
verses.after: There they buried Abraham and his wife Sarah. There they buried Isaac and his wife Rebekah. And there I buried Leah.
verses.tsw_comparator: There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife. There they buried Isaac and Rebekah his wife, and there I buried Leah.

verses.rationale: Keeps the repeated purchase statement as the close of the burial instruction and does not omit the field.
verses.before: The field and the cave that is in it were purchased from the Hittites.”
verses.after: The field and its cave were purchased from the Hittites.”
verses.tsw_comparator: The field and the cave that is in it were purchased from the Hittites.”

verses.rationale: Preserves the physical last movement and gathered-to-people formula without reducing the verse to a bare death notice.
verses.before: When Jacob finished commanding his sons, he drew up his feet into the bed and breathed his last and was gathered to his people.
verses.after: When Jacob finished instructing his sons, he drew his feet up into the bed, breathed his last, and was gathered to his people.
verses.tsw_comparator: When Jacob finished commanding his sons, he drew up his feet into the bed and breathed his last and was gathered to his people.

verses.rationale: Keeps the bodily face-to-face action and all three grief gestures without flattening them to mourning.
verses.before: Then Joseph fell on his father’s face and wept over him and kissed him.
verses.after: Joseph fell over his father’s face, wept over him, and kissed him.
verses.tsw_comparator: Then Joseph fell on his father’s face and wept over him and kissed him.

verses.rationale: Preserves the physicians as Joseph’s servants and their distinct embalming role without labeling them priests.
verses.before: Joseph commanded his servants the physicians to embalm his father. So the physicians embalmed Israel.
verses.after: Joseph ordered the physicians in his service to embalm his father, and the physicians embalmed Israel.
verses.tsw_comparator: And Joseph commanded his servants the physicians to embalm his father. So the physicians embalmed Israel.

verses.rationale: Keeps forty and seventy as distinct periods without adding them together or asserting their precise overlap.
verses.before: Forty days were required for it, for that is how many are required for embalming. And the Egyptians wept for him seventy days.
verses.after: They took forty days, the full time required for embalming. The Egyptians mourned him for seventy days.
verses.tsw_comparator: Forty days were required for it, for that is how many are required for embalming. And the Egyptians wept for him seventy days.

verses.rationale: Retains the indirect request through Pharaoh’s household rather than placing Joseph directly before Pharaoh.
verses.before: And when the days of weeping for him were past, Joseph spoke to the household of Pharaoh, saying, “If now I have found favor in your eyes, please speak in the ears of Pharaoh, saying,
verses.after: When the days of mourning were over, Joseph said to Pharaoh’s household, “If I have found favor with you, please speak to Pharaoh for me. Tell him,
verses.tsw_comparator: And when the days of weeping for him were past, Joseph spoke to the household of Pharaoh, saying, “If now I have found favor in your eyes, please speak in the ears of Pharaoh, saying,

verses.rationale: Preserves the reported oath’s dug wording and Joseph’s return promise; distinguishes the nested father quotation from Joseph’s request without harmonizing it to earlier instructions.
verses.before: ‘My father made me swear, saying, “I am about to die; in my tomb that I hewed out for myself in the land of Canaan, there you will bury me.” Now therefore let me please go up and bury my father. Then I will return.’”
verses.after: ‘My father made me swear an oath. He said, “I am about to die. Bury me in the tomb I dug for myself in Canaan.” Now please let me go up and bury my father. Then I will return.’”
verses.tsw_comparator: ‘My father made me swear, saying, “I am about to die; in my tomb that I hewed out for myself in the land of Canaan, there you shall bury me.” Now therefore let me please go up and bury my father. Then I will return.’”

verses.rationale: Keeps permission grounded in the oath, without adding motives for Pharaoh’s response.
verses.before: Pharaoh answered, “Go up and bury your father, as he made you swear.”
verses.after: Pharaoh answered, “Go up and bury your father, as he made you swear to do.”
verses.tsw_comparator: And Pharaoh answered, “Go up and bury your father, as he made you swear.”

verses.rationale: Retains the full official entourage and elder designations while the list continues across the verse boundary.
verses.before: So Joseph went up to bury his father. With him went up all the servants of Pharaoh, the elders of his household, and all the elders of the land of Egypt,
verses.after: So Joseph went up to bury his father. All Pharaoh’s officials went with him—the elders of his household and all the elders of Egypt—
verses.tsw_comparator: So Joseph went up to bury his father. With him went up all the servants of Pharaoh, the elders of his household, and all the elders of the land of Egypt,

verses.rationale: Keeps all three family groupings and the precise people and animals left behind without inventing a hostage arrangement.
verses.before: as well as all the household of Joseph, his brothers, and his father’s household. Only their little ones and their flocks and their herds were left in the land of Goshen.
verses.after: along with all Joseph’s household, his brothers, and his father’s household. They left only their little ones, flocks, and herds in Goshen.
verses.tsw_comparator: as well as all the household of Joseph, his brothers, and his father’s household. Only their little ones and their flocks and their herds were left in the land of Goshen.

verses.rationale: Preserves both transport/escort groups and the scale of the company without making it a military attack.
verses.before: And there went up with him both chariots and horsemen. It was a very great company.
verses.after: Chariots and horsemen also went up with him. It was an immense company.
verses.tsw_comparator: And there went up with him both chariots and horsemen. It was a very great company.

verses.rationale: Keeps the named threshing floor and beyond-the-Jordan wording without forcing an uncertain route; retains the separate seven-day observance.
verses.before: When they came to the threshing floor of Atad, which is beyond the Jordan, they lamented there with a very great and grievous lamentation, and he made a mourning for his father seven days.
verses.after: When they reached the threshing floor of Atad, beyond the Jordan, they mourned there with loud and bitter lamentation. Joseph observed seven days of mourning for his father.
verses.tsw_comparator: When they came to the threshing floor of Atad, which is beyond the Jordan, they lamented there with a very great and grievous lamentation, and he made a mourning for his father seven days.

verses.rationale: Preserves the local observers’ Egyptian identification and the force of the heavy-mourning idiom and the place-name explanation without changing its uncertain geography.
verses.before: When the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, saw the mourning on the threshing floor of Atad, they said, “This is a grievous mourning by the Egyptians.” Therefore the place was named Abel-mizraim; it is beyond the Jordan.
verses.after: The Canaanites who lived there saw the mourning at the threshing floor of Atad and said, “How deeply the Egyptians are mourning!” That is why the place beyond the Jordan was named Abel-mizraim.
verses.tsw_comparator: When the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, saw the mourning on the threshing floor of Atad, they said, “This is a grievous mourning by the Egyptians.” Therefore the place was named Abel-mizraim; it is beyond the Jordan.

verses.rationale: Keeps the fulfillment summary and identifies the father so the reference remains clear after the place-name aside.
verses.before: Thus his sons did for him as he had commanded them,
verses.after: Jacob’s sons did for him just as he had instructed them.
verses.tsw_comparator: Thus his sons did for him as he had commanded them,

verses.rationale: Preserves the repeated purchase provenance and full cave/field location rather than cutting legally meaningful repetition. Uses facing Mamre consistently with the purchase account in 23:17–19.
verses.before: for his sons carried him to the land of Canaan and buried him in the cave of the field at Machpelah, to the east of Mamre, which Abraham bought with the field from Ephron the Hittite to possess as a burial place.
verses.after: They carried him to Canaan and buried him in the cave in the field of Machpelah, facing Mamre—the field Abraham had bought from Ephron the Hittite as a burial property.
verses.tsw_comparator: for his sons carried him to the land of Canaan and buried him in the cave of the field at Machpelah, to the east of Mamre, which Abraham bought with the field from Ephron the Hittite to possess as a burial place.

verses.rationale: Makes the temporal relation clear while preserving the return of the full accompanying company.
verses.before: After he had buried his father, Joseph returned to Egypt with his brothers and everyone who had gone up with him to bury his father.
verses.after: After burying his father, Joseph returned to Egypt with his brothers and everyone who had gone up with him for the burial.
verses.tsw_comparator: After he had buried his father, Joseph returned to Egypt with his brothers and all who had gone up with him to bury his father.

verses.rationale: Retains renewed fear after reconciliation and the brothers’ acknowledgment of harm rather than claiming forgiveness had removed every tension.
verses.before: When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “It may be that Joseph will hate us and pay us back for all the evil that we did to him.”
verses.after: Now that their father was dead, Joseph’s brothers said, “What if Joseph bears a grudge against us and pays us back for all the harm we did him?”
verses.tsw_comparator: When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “It may be that Joseph will hate us and pay us back for all the evil that we did to him.”

verses.rationale: Presents the paternal command as the brothers’ report without declaring it either fabricated or independently verified.
verses.before: So they sent a message to Joseph, saying, “Your father gave this command before he died:
verses.after: So they sent word to Joseph: “Before your father died, he gave this instruction:
verses.tsw_comparator: So they sent a message to Joseph, saying, “Your father gave this command before he died:

verses.rationale: Keeps offense/sin, the repeated plea, and the religious self-description; distinguishes nested quotation levels and leaves Joseph’s reason for weeping unstated.
